comparator.name: Archaeology
comparator.sourceNotes: The current official programme page accounts for the full 180 EC: 60 EC of compulsory first-year archaeology, 60 EC of compulsory second-year archaeology, and a third year with a 30-EC minor, 10 EC of archaeology theory and data/research design, a 10-EC IMPACT choice and a 10-EC bachelor thesis. It explicitly requires archaeological fieldwork in both first and second year, material conservation and archaeometry, GIS, geoarchaeology, archaeobotany, zooarchaeology and human osteoarchaeology. The programme page presents regional choices inside thematic modules rather than separate formal degree routes, so no route is selected. The 30-EC minor and the 10-EC IMPACT choice remain explicit rather than being populated with invented content.

alternatives.label: Archaeology, ancient societies & material culture
alternatives.concept: Study past societies through world and Greek archaeology, material and visual culture, ancient texts, empires, landscapes, heritage and historical research. Earth observation, soils and data courses contribute bounded landscape and evidence methods, but the programme remains a related-fields route without excavation training, archaeometry, bioarchaeological laboratories or an archaeology thesis.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is led by three archaeology courses and a broader sequence in ancient societies, material and visual culture, landscapes, heritage and historical research. The label names that related-fields composition without claiming a full Archaeology bachelor.
progression: Sustainability, philosophy and imperial history foundations precede archaeology, material-culture, landscape and digital methods. ENSGATE101 precedes Earth Observation, the only formal prerequisite within the programme. Introductory archaeology, art history, literature and data work precede advanced heritage, museum, media and research courses. All courses occur in their exact planned terms; seven are at 300 level.

alternatives.label: Cultural heritage, museums & public memory
alternatives.concept: A distinct heritage route centred on how societies preserve, contest and communicate material culture. It combines archaeology and art history with museums, restitution, public memory, sociology, ethics, rhetoric, documentary practice and humanities research rather than trying to reproduce excavation or bioarchaeology.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum concentrates on museums, heritage ethics, public memory, restitution, community interpretation and documentary communication. The label reflects that institutional and public-facing emphasis.
progression: Foundations in art history, modern history and rhetoric precede archaeology, stylistics, museums and social analysis. Qualitative research, ethics and community communication lead into advanced heritage, public storytelling, persuasion, documentary and humanities research. No selected course has an unmet formal prerequisite, every course occurs in its assigned planned term, and eight courses are at 300 level.
alternatives.distinctness: The heritage route replaces seven courses in environmental science, GIS, soils, data science, ancient literature, philosophy and warfare with seven courses in rhetoric, sociology, qualitative inquiry and ethics. Each programme therefore contains 52.5 EC not present in the other; the substitutions follow from the second route’s public-institutional organising question.

candidates.label: Excavation, archaeological science & bioarchaeology
candidates.assessment: UCR has no excavation sequence, stratigraphy, finds processing, archaeological materials or conservation laboratory, archaeometry, archaeobotany, zooarchaeology or human osteoarchaeology. General GIS, soils, life-science and data courses cannot be relabelled as archaeological field or scientific training.

selection.assessment: Two complete related-fields programmes are defensible. The first studies ancient societies and material culture through UCR archaeology, history, art, landscape and research courses; the second is a distinct public-heritage and museum route. The next generator-backed direction—excavation, archaeological science and bioarchaeology—cannot be implemented at UCR, so production stops at two.

blocks: Both analyse large-scale social and political change; UCR studies empires historically rather than through archaeological evidence.
Both study material evidence and artefacts; UCR offers a broad world-archaeology introduction rather than Groningen’s specialist material-culture module.
Both study Greek and Roman archaeology; UCR provides one course rather than a cumulative Mediterranean sequence.
Both develop data analysis and research design; UCR is general data science rather than archaeological-data analysis.
Both use spatial data and GIS; UCR applies them to environmental observation rather than archaeological sites.
Both use field and earth-science evidence; UCR soils and aquifers does not provide archaeological excavation.
Both connect the classical past to heritage formation and contemporary interpretation.

notes.text: Groningen Archaeology provides cumulative regional archaeology, material and bioarchaeological methods, GIS, two fieldwork sequences, theory and an archaeology thesis. UCR can build coherent related programmes around ancient societies and material culture or heritage, museums and public memory, but neither is a full Archaeology bachelor.

UCR offers three archaeology and ancient-heritage courses but no excavation sequence, stratigraphy, archaeometry, conservation or archaeological-materials laboratory, archaeobotany, zooarchaeology, osteoarchaeology, supervised field school or archaeology thesis. Environmental fieldwork, GIS and data science remain bounded complementary methods rather than substitutes.
